definition: Propagate means to multiply, spread out.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word propagate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know propagate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A single doctored screenshot can propagate through three group chats before breakfast.
Spread stops short of propagate — what spreads gets around, but nothing new is being made along the way.
Disseminate stops short of propagate — disseminating scatters copies from one source, while propagating sets every copy to breeding copies of its own.

Circulate means to move around within a group — a rumor circulates an office, a newsletter makes the rounds. What circulates travels as itself, one copy passing hand to hand. Propagate goes further: whatever propagates mints new copies as it moves, multiplying at every stop.

Reproduce names the single act of making a new copy or a new generation — a cell divides, a photocopier hums. Propagate stresses the spreading that follows: copy after copy moving outward until the signal, the species, or the mistake has covered new ground.

Left alone, the pond's duckweed will propagate until the surface reads solid green: each floating leaf splits into two, two into four, and by the second week the koi are invisible.
Propagate covers both halves of spreading: living things multiplying themselves, and ideas, signals, or errors being passed outward copy by copy.
Either way the heart of it is generation — what propagates doesn't just travel, it reproduces as it goes.
Propagate is the word of gardeners, physicists, and network engineers — cuttings, waves, and updates all propagate.
In loose talk 'spread' will do; choose propagate when the thing multiplies or transmits itself step by step.
Plans and gossip are usually spread; species, signals, and errors propagate.

The starter arrived in Bellhaven in a mason jar, carried home from a bakery workshop by one enthusiastic teacher.
Sourdough starters propagate by division: pour off half, feed the rest, and the poured-off half becomes a new colony that can be handed to a neighbor.
Within a year, the teacher's original jar had descendants in forty kitchens, each one alive, each one feeding new offshoots of its own.
A food writer who traced the lineage called it the town's friendliest invasive species.
The original jar eventually died in a hot car, but by then its loss meant nothing -- the copies had long since outnumbered any need for the source.
